checks.title: A delivery that commits after a later one still reaches the mailbox
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: A delivery that commits after a later one still reaches the mailbox
  Given a mailbox with one registered session
  And delivery A is received before delivery B, but B commits first
  When B commits and the mailbox is pinged
  And A commits a minute later and the mailbox is pinged again
  Then a fresh open of the mailbox lists both messages
  And A's UID is greater than B's
  And no UID was given twice
  And the session was told of each message
proves: SHALL: never losing a delivery that commits late
SHALL: assigning UIDs that only rise
form 01a19daa: a cold read saw a cursor at the newest id lose mail for good (revision 2 finding)
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It takes two deliveries, two pings and an open to show, and the person notices a missing message in their mailbox.

checks.title: The delivery cursor stands ten minutes behind the newest id and only rises
checks.rule: The cursor is the newest delivery id's 48-bit millisecond prefix lowered by 600,000, written dashed as xxxxxxxx-xxxx so it compares as text against the ids, and it is never lowered; rows: a delivery 5 seconds ahead of the cursor is pulled, a delivery at the same prefix sorts above the cursor, and a row read behind the cursor leaves it unchanged.
proves: SHALL: never losing a delivery that commits late
form 01a19daa: Pulling, the cursor rule and its test 'a delivery 5 seconds ahead of the cursor is pulled'
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: The late-commit scenario lands a minute behind, never seconds from the cursor's edge, so only a test of the comparison itself shows a wrong dash or a cursor that falls.

checks.title: One bad delivery does not stop the deliveries after it
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: One bad delivery does not stop the deliveries after it
  Given four deliveries to one mailbox, in order: a good message, one whose stored bytes are gone, one whose bytes cannot be read or stored, and a good message
  When the mailbox pulls
  Then both good messages are in the mailbox in delivery order, with rising UIDs
  And the two bad deliveries are in no one's mailbox
  When a fifth good message is delivered
  Then it arrives in the mailbox with a greater UID
proves: SHALL: never letting one bad message stop later ones
SHALL: pulls deliveries into SQLite
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It takes several deliveries and pulls to show, and the person notices mail that stopped arriving.

checks.title: A held Message-ID gets no UID; none, or one over 998 octets, always gets one
checks.rule: A delivery whose Message-ID of at most 998 octets is already held by a row gets no UID, while a delivery with no Message-ID, or with one over 998 octets, always gets its own UID; the rows are a held id, a repeated missing id, and a repeated 999-octet id under the test wrapper's 2 MB row limit.
proves: toy 01a19d7e: the mailbox DO gives a held Message-ID no UID
SHALL: never letting one bad message stop later ones (an oversized Message-ID must not fail its row against the 2 MB row limit)
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It is one rule shown by a table of fixtures, each a single delivery and pull; the user-facing case of a retry after expunge is in the expunge scenario.

checks.title: Expunge hides a message and keeps it readable until it is erased, and its row after
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: Expunge hides a message and keeps it readable until it is erased, and its row after
  Given a mailbox holding messages with UIDs 1, 2 and 3
  And a session that was told of all three
  When another session expunges UID 3
  Then a fresh open lists UIDs 1 and 2 only
  And the first session can still read UID 3's flags, size, date and bytes
  And a provider's retry of UID 3's message does not bring it back
  And the next new message gets UID 4
  When UID 3's bytes are erased
  Then the first session can still read UID 3's flags, size and date, and reads its bytes as nothing
  And no message ever gets UID 3 again
proves: SHALL: keeping an expunged message's bytes readable until they are erased (FR-MAIL-053) and its row after that
SHALL: assigning UIDs that only rise
rfc3501.2.3.1.1: a UID is never reused
toy 01a19d7e: the mailbox DO never reuses a UID
toy 01a1a4ad: keep the tombstone, since removing the row closes a woken session with 1011
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It is a sequence of expunge, open, reads, a redelivery and an erasure, and the person meets each outcome in their mail app.

checks.title: Reading the rows a view names works past 100 messages
checks.rule: held passes the UIDs as one JSON parameter, so a request for 101 UIDs, expunged or not, succeeds under the Durable Object SQLite limit of 100 bound parameters that the test wrapper enforces.
proves: SHALL: keeping an expunged message's ... row (readable to a woken session)
form 01a19daa: a cold read saw a held query break every mailbox over 100 messages on waking (revision 2 finding)
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It is one call against a platform limit that only the test wrapper reproduces, and no scenario above holds 101 messages.

checks.title: A rebuilt mailbox object takes a greater UIDVALIDITY
checks.rule: uid_validity is set once, when the mailbox object's tables are created, from the current time in seconds, so a fresh object for a mailbox whose deliveries outlived the old one reports a greater uid_validity than the old one did.
proves: rfc3501.2.3.1.1: UIDVALIDITY must be greater if UIDs fail to persist
SHALL: assigning UIDs that only rise
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: Losing an object's SQLite is not something any user does through a surface, so the rule is shown on two fresh objects with a controlled clock.

checks.title: Overlapping pulls give each delivery one UID, and a pull asked during one runs again
checks.rule: Pulls are single-flight: two pulls asked for at once give each delivery, with or without a Message-ID, exactly one UID, and a pull asked for while one runs runs once more after it, so a row committed during the first pull is pulled without waiting for the alarm.
proves: SHALL: one Durable Object ... assigning UIDs
SHALL: tell every registered IMAP session of any change (without a five-minute wait for the alarm)
form 01a19daa: Tests, 'two overlapping pulls with no Message-ID add each row once, and a ping during a pull is not missed'
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: The race needs control of when a pull's read and a commit interleave, which no sequence of calls through the surface gives.

checks.title: Every change reaches every session on the mailbox, whoever caused it
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: Every change reaches every session on the mailbox, whoever caused it
  Given a person's Mac idling on their inbox and their iPhone with the inbox selected
  When new mail is delivered and the iPhone's SELECT finds it before any ping arrives
  Then the Mac is told of the new message, with the UID the iPhone sees
  When another message is delivered and pinged
  Then both the Mac and the iPhone are told of it
  When the iPhone flags a message and then expunges one
  Then the Mac is told of the flag change and of the expunge
proves: SHALL: tell every registered IMAP session of any change
SHALL: keep each mailbox in one Durable Object (both sessions see one set of UIDs)
form 01a19daa: Pulling, 'whenever a pull adds a row, from any caller, every registered session is told', or an iPhone's SELECT leaves the Mac unaware
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It takes two sessions and several commands, and the person notices a Mac that never shows mail the iPhone already has.

checks.title: No command waits for a tell, and one dead session holds up no one
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: No command waits for a tell, and one dead session holds up no one
  Given four sessions on one mailbox: one idling, one in the middle of a command, one whose connection never answers, and one whose connection fails every tell
  When new mail arrives and the session in the middle of a command runs a SELECT that finds it
  Then the SELECT completes without waiting for any session to be told
  And a ping, a flag change and an expunge each complete while tells are still outstanding
  And the idling session is told of the new message
  When another message arrives
  Then the idling session and the one whose tells fail are each told of it, despite the session that never answers
proves: SHALL: without ever waiting for the telling
SHALL: tell every registered IMAP session of any change
form 01a19daa: a cold read saw a tell cycle hang a mailbox and every ping for good (revision 3 finding)
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: The hang shows only across a session's command, the mailbox's pull and another session's tell together, and every person on the mailbox notices it as mail that stops.

checks.title: Mail nobody announced still arrives, even across a delivery store outage
checks.gherkin:
Scenario: Mail nobody announced still arrives, even across a delivery store outage
  Given a mailbox with one session idling
  And a delivery whose ping was lost
  And a flag change that committed but whose tell was lost when the object stopped
  And the delivery store fails when the next timed check runs
  When the delivery store recovers and the following timed check runs
  Then the idling session is told of the new message and of the flag change
proves: SHALL: never losing a delivery
SHALL: tell every registered IMAP session of any change
form 01a19daa: alarm() re-arms first so a D1 outage cannot end the chain, and tell-owed makes an untold commit heard
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: It needs a lost ping, a lost tell, a failing dependency and two timed checks in sequence, and the person notices mail that never shows up.

checks.title: A tell left running after its call returns reaches an idle session on deployed Cloudflare
checks.rule: On the deploy issue for examples/imap: deliver a message to a mailbox with an idle session through the bridge, and the session hears it; the run records the time from delivery to the untagged EXISTS, never asserting it.
proves: SHALL: tell every registered IMAP session of any change without ever waiting for the telling (the tell runs in ctx.waitUntil after the RPC returns)
form 01a19daa: event 8, shown locally only
checks.why_not_the_other_kind: Whether work in waitUntil outlives its RPC is a property of the deployed runtime that local workerd cannot settle.

gaps.failure_way: A delivery commits more than ten minutes after the time in its UUIDv7 id, so it sorts behind the cursor and no pull reads it
gaps.question: The SHALL says a late commit is never lost and the form keeps the cursor ten minutes behind. Is there a proven bound on how late a delivery can commit (a receiving Worker's wall-clock limit, for instance) that makes ten minutes enough, and if not, what reads a delivery that commits later than that?

gaps.failure_way: A transient failure reading one row (R2 get throwing, a D1 hiccup) is recorded as unreadable, and the delivery is skipped for good
gaps.question: Conflict between 'never letting one bad message stop later ones' and 'never losing a delivery': the form records any failure on a row as unreadable so later rows pull, which also loses a good message on a transient error. Does a failed row retry, how many times and how is it told apart from a bad message, or can a skipped delivery be pulled again later?

left_out.why: Read as the rules require: it decides IMAP logins (adapter strategies, PBKDF2, rate limits) and settles no outcome of this requirement, so no check traces to it.

left_out.candidate: A bad delivery is not read from R2 again on the next pull
left_out.why: Re-reading costs reads but breaks no SHALL; it is bookkeeping of the skipped table, an implementation detail.
Telling with nothing to report breaks no SHALL; it is an economy, not this requirement.

left_out.why: Registration lifecycle breaks no SHALL here: a dead name costs alarms, and every live session is still told. It belongs to the session object's requirement.
